idiom_name: abstract base class raising NotImplementedError, or a module carrying the skeleton over hook methods
implementation_notes: Ruby has no abstract methods and no compile phase, so the skeleton is a plain method that calls step methods: required steps are declared by convention and raise NotImplementedError (mostly a documentation aid, since calling an unimplemented step raises NoMethodError anyway), or the whole skeleton lives in a module that is included into the class - the more idiomatic carrier because it does not force a class hierarchy (Module#include is documented in the core Module docs). Blocks and yield replace the pattern entirely when only one step varies, and super lets an overridden hook extend its default; keep the classic form when several steps vary together and the shared state belongs to one object.
code_sketch:
module ImportPipeline
  def run(source)
    rows = parse(source)          # required step
    before_store(rows)            # hook: default no-op
    store(rows)                   # required step
  end

  def parse(source) = raise NotImplementedError, "parse must be overridden"
  def before_store(rows); end
  def store(rows) = raise NotImplementedError, "store must be overridden"
end
pitfalls: NotImplementedError-raising steps are documentation, not enforcement: because Ruby resolves methods at call time, a forgotten step fails with NoMethodError halfway through the algorithm instead of at load time.
A module mixin's step methods are looked up on the including class, so a name clash silently shadows a step - keep step names prefixed or namespaced.
A hook that calls super needs a concrete default in the module; if any layer of a chain forgets super, the layers beneath it are skipped without a warning.
